reason: The sources provide over a dozen cross-verified facts across independent scientific institutions documenting R Coronae Borealis and its unique soot-induced fading behavior.
story: In the constellation Corona Borealis sits a rare yellow supergiant star that defies the normal rules of astronomy. Most variable stars grab attention by dramatically flaring up into novae, but R Coronae Borealis does the exact opposite: it periodically chokes on its own atmosphere. Normally shining just bright enough to see with the naked eye at sixth magnitude, the star abruptly plunges into near-invisibility at unpredictable intervals, dropping up to nine magnitudes—fading by a factor of nearly a million. First discovered by English astronomer Edward Pigott in 1795, this 'reverse nova' is starved of hydrogen and smothered in carbon. Pulsations and shockwaves cause carbon gas in its upper atmosphere to condense into thick clouds of actual soot. While visible light is almost completely extinguished by these carbon smoke puffs, infrared light cuts right through the smog. Eventually, radiation pressure clears the cosmic exhaust, allowing the star to reappear.
angle: Instead of exploding brighter like a normal nova, this supergiant repeatedly vanishes from naked-eye sight because its atmosphere condenses into clouds of pure soot, choking out 99.999% of its visible light.

claims.claim: R Coronae Borealis is a low-mass supergiant star.
R Coronae Borealis is the prototype star of the R Coronae Borealis class of variable stars.
The variability of R Coronae Borealis was discovered by English astronomer Edward Pigott.
R Coronae Borealis variables are hydrogen-deficient and carbon-rich.
R Coronae Borealis normally shines at approximately magnitude 6, making it visible to the naked eye.
The star undergoes irregular, unpredictable drops in brightness.
During fading events, R Coronae Borealis can plunge to 15th magnitude, dropping by up to 8 to 9 magnitudes.
Because it fades dramatically instead of brightening during outbursts, it earned the nickname 'reverse nova'.
The sudden fading is caused by carbon gas rapidly condensing into clouds of dust or soot that block visible light.
While visible light dims dramatically, infrared brightness remains largely unchanged because infrared waves penetrate the dust.
The star gradually returns to maximum brightness as stellar radiation pressure disperses the soot.
Only about 150 R Coronae Borealis variables are currently known in the Milky Way galaxy.
A leading formation theory is the merger of two white dwarf stars, specifically a helium white dwarf and a carbon-oxygen white dwarf.
Another competing model for their formation is a final helium shell flash in an evolved star.
In August 2007, R Coronae Borealis began an unprecedented decade-long fade that bottomed out around magnitude 15.2.

disputed: Location of dust condensation: One model places soot formation at roughly 20 stellar radii where temperatures drop to 1,500 K, while another argues shocks near the photosphere drive immediate cooling and condensation (attribute as competing models).

Origin of the extended circumstellar shell: Sources debate whether the massive dust shell represents a fossil planetary nebula from a final helium flash, remnants of a white dwarf merger, or steady mass loss over roughly 10,000 years during the RCB phase (attribute: 'scientists debate whether the surrounding shell is an ancient planetary nebula or merger debris').

Estimated total number of RCB stars in the Milky Way: S2 notes up to 1,000 are expected despite only ~150 known, while S7 remarks that fewer than 50 are known due to short lifespans (rely strictly on the verified ~150 known stars and leave out the theoretical total).
